entries.note: Often traced to ancient Greek elections using beans, but the phrase only appears in 20th-century America, and Greeks actually voted with pebbles (hence [[psephology]]).
The study of elections, from the Greek word for pebble, because ancient Greeks dropped pebbles into jars when voting.
To reveal gossip on purpose, unlike the accidental [[spill the beans]]; it comes from late-20th-century Black drag culture, where 'T' meant truth, and Lady Chablis used it in 1994.
The French [[spill the beans]], picturing a mine whose fuse was accidentally left sticking out, showing where the bomb is.
The Spanish [[spill the beans]]; the hosts aren't sure what the secret cake refers to.

entries.term: now the monkey comes out of the sleeve
entries.original: nu komt de aap uit de mouw
entries.translation: now the monkey comes out of the sleeve
entries.note: The Dutch [[spill the beans]], possibly from a magic trick, with a more magician-like version of [[let the cat out of the bag]] energy.

entries.term: let the cat out of the bag
entries.note: Covered in an earlier episode: it isn't about the cat-o'-nine-tails but about buying a [[pig in a poke]] and finding a worthless cat inside.
'Not my cup of tea' dates to 1908 and was popularized by Punch in the 1930s; it rests on everyone liking their tea differently.

entries.term: not for all the tea in China
entries.note: Late-19th-century phrase meaning under no circumstances or at no price, because tea was a costly import.
A slightly newer version of [[tempest in a teapot]], with the same idea.
Goes back to the early 1800s, a little earlier than [[storm in a teacup]].
Slang for coffee first recorded in the 1930s, probably from [[jamoke]]; the Josephus Daniels navy alcohol ban theory lacks evidence, and the average-Joe idea is also unlikely.
Late-19th-century American slang for coffee, a blend of [[java]] and [[mocha]], and the likely source of [[cup of joe]].
Rob says Dick, like Jack and Joe, was a popular everyman name, which is why we have things like spotted dick.
Originally just a person's name, now used for any person, another example of everyman names.
1800s stable slang for horses fed on beans before a race or hunt and in fit condition; it once also meant arrogant or purse-proud.

entries.original: parler français comme une vache espagnole
entries.translation: to speak like a Spanish cow
entries.note: Said of someone speaking a language badly; Rob notes it's offensive to learners, to the Spanish and to cows.
In Old English, apple meant any fruit and 'the apple of the eye' meant the [[pupil]]; it translates a Hebrew phrase meaning 'little man of the eye' and appears in Shakespeare.
Rob says it describes a little person, from the tiny reflection of yourself you see in someone else's eye, which ties in with [[apple of my eye]].
From Cleopatra's line in Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra: being green and cold like lettuce means naive, like unripe fruit.
Taken from French, where it meant lettuce, and further back from the Roman sense of salted; Rob notes that in Germany it covers anything heavy with mayonnaise.
Cockney rhyming slang for stairs, which Rob thinks of before [[apples and oranges]].
Replaced the older [[apples and oysters]] in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, first for false equivalences between similar-looking things, though now used for very different things.
The original 17th-century comparison, recorded by John Ray, for two utterly dissimilar things, later displaced by [[apples and oranges]].
The saying that one rotten apple spoils the rest appears in a 1528 Reformation pamphlet and, earlier, a 1340 Kentish moral treatise.
Supposedly coined in 1976 by Tom Iacino, probably a pun on [[boob tube]] watchers as 'tubers'; other theories involve slouching or being vegetative.
1970s slang for the television, whose watchers became 'boob tubers', the likely pun behind [[couch potato]]; in Britain it's also a 1990s garment.

entries.term: how do you like them apples
entries.note: Found in 1895 in Texas's Bryan Daily Eagle, boasting about cotton receipts; the WWI toffee-apple mortar story is too late to be the source.
Literally means [[pomegranate]], which grenades resemble, and when they explode bits burst out like pomegranate seeds.
Means 'grainy apple', with the first part matching French pomme, apple; the source of [[grenade]].
19th-century slang for something desirable or sure; it stuck to New York after sportswriter John J. Fitz Gerald used it in 1921 for the city's rich racetracks.
The usual explanation is that someone wanting a fight would put a wood chip on their shoulder and dare others to knock it off.
American, first recorded in 1891, so not from OED editor C. T. Onions; the Cockney rhyming slang onion rings = things is possible but puzzling.
Jess says it comes from Cockney rhyming slang; Rob says it's about the only rhyming slang that has caught on in the United States.
Cockney rhyming slang for the telephone, given as an example of rhyming slang in everyday British speech.
Rob rejects the claim that it was a cannonball rack that shed its balls in the cold; no nautical guides he checked mention such a thing.
Dates to at least the early 1900s and was adapted into [[go bananas]].
Adapted from [[go ape]] by linking monkeys with bananas, with 'bananas' alone recorded from the 1920s, though wild monkeys rarely eat bananas.
1920s slang for nonsense, named after banana-scented amyl acetate, an artificial chemical; Rube Goldberg popularized it in his comic strips.
Jess recalls, from memory and with uncertainty, Old West con men selling oil said to repel snakes.

entries.term: the proof of the pudding is in the eating
entries.note: 'Proof' uses the old meaning 'test', as in proving ground, and the pudding was stuffed entrails, like haggis, which you had to eat to judge.
A 19th-century phrase, probably a pun on [[umbles|umble pie]], a lowly dish of deer entrails given to servants.
Deer entrails baked into umble pie for servants after a hunt, eaten long before the pun [[humble pie]] appeared.
Means perfect order, first recorded in the 1780s diary of a British naval officer; one theory says it mishears French nappe pliée, a folded cloth.
Built up through Johnny Appleseed, early American cookbooks, pie as a symbol of prosperity, and WWII soldiers fighting for 'mom and apple pie'.
Found in the 16th century and common across Europe, probably from Ecclesiastes 10:20, where a bird of the air carries your voice.
From Aesop's fox, who calls the grapes he can't reach sour; it became an idiom around the 1760s, and Mark Twain revived it in Tom Sawyer.
